78: A production day always follows the same order, and that order is a food safety matter, not a matter of taste. You receive the pasteurized base from your licensed dairy at 41 °F (5 °C) or colder and write down the lot code. Then you flavor it and fold in the mix-ins; after the dairy's pasteurization you add only flavorings and mix-ins, with no raw eggs and no raw milk or cream, and custard flavors come from a custard base. Next the mix goes through the batch freezer, where it is drawn at about 16-19 °F, and then into the hardening cabinet until it reaches 0 °F (−18 °C) or colder at the core. It is stored at 0 °F or colder and served from the dipping cabinet at 6-10 °F, depending on the manufacturer. Date-mark the base when you open it (Food Code 3-501.17), label every tub with its batch date and note each batch with its date, lot code and temperatures: that log is the backbone of your written food safety plan. If you decide to pasteurize your own mix, which is the variant and needs a state license and other equipment, fats, egg yolks and emulsifiers go in before pasteurization, never after.
79: The heart of the production room is a short list of equipment. A 20-qt horizontal batch freezer costs {{inv_batch_freezer}} in the case: a Carpigiani of that size lists at about $40,800, so this is a Kit estimate on the low side, reconditioned units cost less and you should get at least two quotes before you close the loan. The hardening cabinet is {{inv_hardening}}, the storage freezers {{inv_congeladores}} and the dipping cabinets for {{sabores}} flavors {{inv_dipping}}: two ventilated modules, with room for the flavor of the day or a reserve. The base refrigerator and flavor prep cost {{inv_base_frio}}, and the front counter with dipper wells, espresso and waffle cone irons {{inv_mostrador}}. There is no pasteurizer in the budget, because the case buys a pasteurized base from a licensed dairy. Always ask for a quote with installation and delivery time, because the price changes by brand.
80: With this equipment, the production room covers the summer with {{produccion_horas}} hours of production a day before opening, plus an extra shift in July, the month with the most sales; the cash flow tab marks the peak. The batch freezer, the hardening cabinet and the freezers leave room for the cakes and the catering orders. A quality note: federal rules set a minimum weight of 4.5 lb per gallon for ice cream (21 CFR 135.110), but a well-made craft ice cream usually has less air and more flavor, and a gelato-style product is denser. In winter the cabinets drop to 10-12 flavors, which reduces waste and electricity.
81: The schedule follows the season. From mid-April to September, with the peak from Memorial Day to Labor Day, you open long hours every day. In March, the first half of April and October you open fewer hours and six days a week. From November to February you open short weekday hours, longer on weekends, closed on Mondays, with three weeks off from mid-January. The installation asks for about 30 kW of 3-phase service (batch freezer, hardening cabinet, air conditioning and the cabinets running day and night): ask the utility about 3-phase service and amps before signing the lease. Utilities average {{suministros_mes}} a month in the case, and summer pushes them up.
82: Prevent cross-contact with one scoop per tub and a dipper well with running water (Food Code 3-304.12). The cabinet runs at the temperature your food safety plan sets, usually 6-10 °F depending on the manufacturer; storage is at 0 °F or colder and melted ice cream is never refrozen. Expect some waste in production, and measure it every week. The cold chain is kept up with a refrigeration service contract with an EPA 608-certified technician. Packaging is free of expanded polystyrene, and spoons are paper or compostable.
85: The team in the case is small and spread across the seasons. You are the ice cream maker and general manager, full time: recipes, balancing, production and control of the production room. Next to you is a shift lead who also works the counter all year. For the season there is a seasonal scooper from April to September, full time in those months, a summer scooper from June to August, and a production assistant from May to September. Relief cover for vacations and days off completes the picture: {{plantilla_puestos}} positions in all. You are paid below what a hired manager would earn, so plan to draw in addition from net profit.
86: That team adds up to {{plantilla_jornadas}} full-time equivalents and costs {{personal_a1}} in year 1, including employer payroll taxes of {{cargas_pct}}: {{personal_pct}} of sales. It is the biggest expense of the business, above the rent, so it pays to measure it well. The schedule covers {{cobertura_horas}} of the hours the shop needs: you cover what is needed, with a small margin. The plan budgets $15 an hour or more and does not model tips. In years 2 and 3 the payroll grows with people you add on the "Staffing" tab, not with a percentage. Look at that percentage calmly: in an ice cream shop, labor is the lever that weighs most on the result, and every counter hour that does not sell is paid just the same. That is why the seasonal staff come in only when the season needs them, and the owner covers with their own work the more technical hours in the production room.
87: Seasonal staff are hired as seasonal W-2 employees, with an offer letter that states the expected start and end of the season, and rehired every spring. They are covered by workers' compensation and by state unemployment insurance like any other employee. It is not a one-season relationship: the person does not disappear in October, comes back when you call, and that helps you keep the craft you have trained. Think of it as an investment: someone who already knows how to serve without mixing flavors and how to work the cabinets saves you mistakes and waste in July.
88: The federal minimum wage is $7.25 an hour, and your state or city may set a higher one; the case budgets $15 an hour or more, so enter your own floor on "0. Assumptions". Keep time records for all staff (FLSA). Teen scoopers aged 14 and 15 may work only within the hours of 29 CFR 570.35: outside school hours, 3 hours on a school day and 18 in a school week, and until 9 pm from June 1 through Labor Day; some states add work permits, so check yours. And a warning: never replace staff with contractors who invoice you. If you set the schedule and give the orders, that is misclassification and a penalty waiting to happen. Your CPA can confirm how to classify a specific person, such as a part-time production assistant, before the first day and not after the first audit.
89: In July and August the schedule is tight: the owner works extra hours or a weekend extra comes in. Decide from the start who covers those weeks, because improvising in the middle of summer ends in fatigue, mistakes in the production room and long lines. If you hire minors, remember the hour limits above and check your state's rules before signing, especially for evening shifts. And leave a margin of rest for yourself: the exhausted ice cream maker in August is the one who changes a recipe without weighing it or skips a temperature check.
90: Train the team before opening. The person in charge of each shift needs the Certified Food Protection Manager certification (Food Code 2022, 2-102.12; states still on an older edition ask for at least one certified manager), and the others a food handler card where your state requires one, covering temperatures, allergens and the order of the production day. Besides that, the ice cream maker needs technical training in mix balancing, because a badly balanced recipe gives an icy or hard ice cream. And count on OSHA basics: cold, lifting and cuts are the typical accidents of a production room. Schedule a short refresher at the start of each season, when the seasonal staff return, because what is not repeated is forgotten; that way everyone who arrives in April already knows the order of the production room and the allergens of each flavor.
93: To open you need {{inversion_total}} in total cash. That is {{capex}} of startup costs, which include the build-out, the equipment and the launch (training, branding, permits and opening inventory), the security deposit, the rent before opening and a contingency on the build-out, plus {{fondo_maniobra}} of working capital. There is no credit for sales tax paid on purchases, so nothing is added for it. The cash need of {{necesidad_caja}} is financed with {{fondos_propios}} of your own money ({{aportacion_pct}}) and a {{prestamo}} SBA 7(a) loan at {{tipo_prestamo}} over {{plazo_prestamo}} years, a nominal rate and not APR, with no interest-only period. The annual loan payment is {{cuota_anual}}. Lenders usually expect an owner equity injection, often around 10% for SBA start-ups, though many want 20-30%.
94: The three-year P&L projects revenue of {{ventas_a1}}, {{ventas_a2}} and {{ventas_a3}}. The {{clientes_dia}} customers a day are the average of year 1 with the opening included: the Excel spreads the year with seasonality and a start-up ramp, but the year bills what the P&L says. Customers grow, not the price: {{crecimiento_a2}} more in year 2 and {{crecimiento_a3}} in year 3, from {{clientes_dia}} to {{clientes_a2}} and {{clientes_a3}} customers a day at the same average check of {{ticket}} excl. sales tax. In year 1 the gross margin is {{margen_bruto_pct}}, with cost of goods sold at {{cogs_pct}} of sales, labor at {{personal_a1}} ({{personal_pct}}) and rent at {{ocupacion_anual}} ({{ocupacion_pct}}); prime cost is {{prime_cost_pct}}. EBITDA is {{ebitda_a1}}, a {{ebitda_pct_a1}} margin. Net profit is {{resultado_neto_a1}}, {{resultado_neto_a2}} and {{resultado_neto_a3}}, a net margin of {{margen_neto_a1}} in year 1. The book applies an effective income tax rate of {{impuesto_beneficios}}, the prudent side; an LLC taxed as a pass-through pays through your personal return, so confirm it with your CPA. These are ice cream shop margins: tight, and dependent on filling the summer.
95: Accounting break-even is at {{equilibrio_clientes_dia}} customers a day, with revenue of {{equilibrio_ventas}} a year. Cash break-even, which also covers the loan payments and leaves depreciation out, is at {{equilibrio_caja_clientes_dia}} customers a day, or {{equilibrio_caja_ventas}} a year, and the margin of safety over it is {{holgura_caja_pct}}. Because the loan is repaid from the first month, there is no interest-only year to flatter the first result. Check the margin on the "Break-Even" tab for each year: those are the years to watch, because there is no room for a bad summer without touching the cash.
96: The cash flow numbers the months from 1 to 12, and Month 1 is March. The ramp-up starts below full pace and reaches cruising speed in a few months. The lowest cash balance of the year, {{saldo_minimo}}, comes in Month {{mes_saldo_minimo}}, just after the investment is paid. Then summer adds and winter subtracts: from November to February only a small share of the year's sales comes in while fixed costs stay flat, so cash falls month by month, and that is why the plan never opens in the fall. The summer pays for the winter. The model spreads payroll over twelve months even though seasonal staff are paid only in season: winter looks more expensive and summer cheaper than in real life. The balances of March and February barely change, but from June to January your real cash will be lower than the tab shows, and it recovers little by little.
97: The DSCR is {{dscr_a1}} in year 1 and never drops below {{dscr_min}}, against a limit of {{dscr_limite}} in the workbook and a typical lender target of {{dscr_objetivo}}: the business covers its debt with room to spare in the example, but a bad summer would shrink it quickly, and that is why a lender will want to see your winter plan. The project payback before debt is {{payback}}, so this is not a quick-return investment. Treat it as a craft business that pays you a modest draw and returns the capital with patience.
98: The pessimistic scenario is a cool, rainy summer: {{pesimista_clientes}} customers a day at {{pesimista_ticket}} over {{pesimista_dias}} days give revenue of {{pesimista_ventas}} and a pre-tax loss of {{pesimista_perdida}}. In the optimistic one, {{optimista_clientes}} customers at {{optimista_ticket}} over {{optimista_dias}} days leave a pre-tax result of {{optimista_resultado}} on revenue of {{optimista_ventas}}. The distance between the two is what separates a good summer from a bad one. In the pessimistic case, the estimated closing cash of year 1 is {{pesimista_caja}}.
99: There are two reasoned alternatives, with no Excel behind them. The first is the make-your-own-mix variant: a batch pasteurizer costs roughly $25,000-45,000 (get quotes), and you also need a state dairy plant or frozen dessert manufacturer license, 3-A equipment and inspections; in that variant, fats, egg yolks and emulsifiers go in before pasteurization and the mix must reach at least 155 °F for 30 minutes or 175 °F for 25 seconds (Ohio rule 901:11-3-05, as one example). Your state sets its own rules: ask your state department of agriculture. The second alternative is closing from November to February: you save part of the labor and utilities, but the rent keeps running, and you lose the holiday cakes, the pre-orders and the winter customers. Put the real prices of whatever you choose on the "Startup Costs" tab.
102: You can open as an LLC, or as an S corporation if your CPA recommends it, and you register with an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS. You also need your state payroll and unemployment registration, a business license from your city or county and a sales tax permit from your state; the example uses one sales tax rate of {{sales_tax}}. Requirements are set at four levels (federal, state, county and city) and change from one place to another, so check with your state and local offices.
103: Do a zoning check before signing the lease: confirm that the address allows retail food with on-site production, ask the utility about 3-phase service and amps, and ask the city what a patio needs. The build-out needs a building permit and ends in a certificate of occupancy. Before you build, your local health department reviews the plans with the equipment layout (plan review, Food Code 8-201.11). Outdoor tables are public right-of-way and need a separate sidewalk café or patio permit, and the sign may need a signage permit; the fee in the Excel is an example that you must replace with your city's. The electrical work also needs an inspection.
104: The license decision comes first, and it depends on your state. Buying pasteurized base from a licensed dairy is the lighter route, while making your own mix usually adds a state dairy plant or frozen dessert manufacturer license, 3-A equipment and inspections. In Vermont, for example, freezing a pasteurized base needs a Frozen Dessert License from the Agency of Agriculture, and only flavorings may be added after pasteurization, while blending your own mix needs a Milk Handler License. In Georgia, a retailer that freezes a mix from a licensed dairy processor is exempt from the Dairy Manufacturer's License only for ice cream eaten on the premises: ask before you sell pints to go, delivery or catering. Arizona, Massachusetts and Pennsylvania treat it differently, so check. Ask your state department of agriculture in writing before you sign the lease, and then apply for your health permit with your local health department.
105: Your food safety plan is built on the FDA Food Code as your state has adopted it. The person in charge holds the Certified Food Protection Manager certification (2-102.12 in the 2022 Food Code; older editions ask for at least one certified manager), and food handler cards apply depending on your state. Dipper wells have running water (3-304.12), cold holding is 41 °F (5 °C) or colder, storage is at 0 °F or colder and the base is date-marked when opened (3-501.17), with every tub labeled with its batch date. Pints you package in the shop need a label (3-602.11). The case uses no raw egg, because the base is a pasteurized base from a licensed dairy. Ice cream that melts is never refrozen, and your plan, not a national rule, sets the cabinet temperature together with the manufacturer's specification. Your local health department has the final word on how it applies to you.
106: Names matter. "Ice cream" under 21 CFR 135.110 means at least 10% milkfat and at least 4.5 lb per gallon, and "frozen custard" needs 1.4% egg yolk solids. Gelato is not named in that rule: if you call it ice cream, the federal standard applies. Honest claims protect you: write "made here in small batches" when it is true, and use "homemade" or "house-made" only when you really make it in the shop.
107: The 9 major allergens, including sesame since 2023 (FASTER Act), must be handled with care. Scoops and dipper wells are shared, so never promise allergen-free. Sales tax works state by state: the scoop to eat on site or to go is generally taxed as prepared food, while a packaged pint or a whole cake may be taxed as a grocery in some states (the Texas Comptroller is one example). Use your blended rate and check your state.
108: On staffing, the federal rules are the FLSA, the hour limits for ages 14 and 15 (29 CFR 570.35), your state minimum wage and the seasonal W-2 rules. Insure with equipment breakdown and food spoilage, license any music you play (ASCAP, BMI and SESAC) and let only an EPA 608-certified technician handle refrigerant. This section covers what we can state; for everything else, check with your state and local offices before you decide. A note for the UK: register the food business with your local council at least 28 days before opening, expect a Food Hygiene Rating of 0 to 5 (the FHIS scheme in Scotland), check with HMRC how VAT applies to what you sell, and declare the 14 allergens.
111: The conclusion is that an ice cream shop of this size is viable, but demanding. With {{clientes_dia}} customers a day at {{ticket}} per person, year 1 leaves a net profit of {{resultado_neto_a1}} and a cash margin of {{holgura_caja_pct}}. The lowest DSCR is {{dscr_min}}, the lowest cash balance is {{saldo_minimo}} in Month {{mes_saldo_minimo}}, March, and the payback is {{payback}}. This is not a business to start with tight capital.
112: The first risk is opening in the fall. The plan opens in March so that the summer cash reaches the first winter; if you open in October, you spend the working capital for five or six months before the first summer. The second is winter cash: from November to February only a small share of the year's sales comes in while fixed costs stay flat, and without a winter plan the numbers do not work. Reduce it with ice cream cakes and holiday pies to order, hot chocolate, holiday pints and catering. Closing from November to February is an alternative, not a magic recipe.
113: The third is the wrong space. A single-phase space when you need about 30 kW of 3-phase service, with no ventilation for the condensers or no floor sinks, costs you a service upgrade, time and money. Check all of that before signing the lease and ask the utility about 3-phase service and amps. The fourth is an oversized cabinet: more flavors than a mid-size city can sell only adds waste and power, so the plan runs {{sabores}} in summer and 10-12 in winter. The fifth is waste and refrigeration failures: a failure in August is a tub lost for every flavor. Buy insurance with equipment breakdown and food spoilage, and sign a service contract with a refrigeration technician.
114: The sixth risk is the weather: a cool, rainy summer is the pessimistic scenario, with a loss. It cannot be avoided: in such a year revenue falls from {{ventas_a1}} to {{pesimista_ventas}} and the pre-tax result turns into a loss of {{pesimista_perdida}}, more than the cash margin of {{holgura_caja_pct}} can absorb. A bad summer can be survived; two in a row cannot without renegotiating the loan payment. The seventh is raw materials that spike, such as pistachio, cocoa and vanilla. Cost out every flavor, review the menu price every season and do not let a star flavor eat your margin. When an ingredient spikes you have three exits: raise the price of that flavor, rotate it as a seasonal flavor or replace it with another that gives the same appeal. What you cannot do is keep selling it at the same price without looking at the cost. Insurance does not cover a bad summer, so the real protection is a plan with a cash cushion and a working capital reserve that you do not touch for anything else.
115: Four common mistakes are avoided with a little method. Writing "homemade" or "small-batch" on the sign when the ice cream is not made in the shop, or calling something "ice cream" or "frozen custard" when the recipe does not meet 21 CFR 135.110, is misleading: use only what you can prove. Signing the lease before you decide how you will get your base, buying it from a licensed dairy or making your own mix, can leave you with a space that does not fit your license. Hiring the summer late, or with contractors instead of seasonal W-2 employees, complicates your team and exposes you to a penalty. And unbalanced recipes give icy or hard textures: technical training is an investment, not an expense. Review these four points with your team before opening and come back to them at the start of each season, because they are the ones most forgotten when work piles up.
116: The action plan has six phases and 80 tasks in the checklist that comes with the kit. Phase 1 is business setup and taxes, with 12 tasks. Phase 2, site and permits, has 15. Phase 3, production and health, has 15. Phase 4, staff and food safety, has 12. Phase 5, brand and menu, has 13. And phase 6, opening and season, has another 13. Follow the order: the zoning check, the electrical service and the license decision come before any equipment purchase, and the health permit before the first batch. Check off each task when you close it, and if one slips, see which others depend on it before you move the opening date.
117: The next step is to fill in the Excel with your own numbers: your real rent, your average check, your loan, your staff and your opening calendar. Change only the green cells; this document reflects the example case, and yours is set by your spreadsheet. With your own data in front of you, come back to this section and check what is left in cash if your second summer turns out like the pessimistic scenario. If the cash holds up, you have a solid plan to take to your lender; if not, adjust the investment, the calendar or the size of your equipment before you sign anything.
